You will carry a dog’s tongue placed in your shoe under your big toe, or if you carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to Sextus; or hare’s hair or dung, according to Pliny. Or you will carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or you will give it a frog in a morsel of food; all these things are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs flee the sight of a man all day long if he expels a tick from a dog and carries it for a little while. Oppian:

> *But if you carry a small piece of a hyena’s skin*
> *Cut away, immediately the puppies and fierce dogs*
> *Struck with sharp terror, will not bark at you*
> *As you approach, even if they were barking before.*

### *So that a dog cannot run.*

If you smear its wings with oil, it will be hindered in its running; this will happen in this way.

### *So that a hawk may be spirited.*

You will animate the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food it uses during the hunting season with wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from its beak into a dove chick, then make it fly. Thus:

### *You will make partridges more combative,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight. From this, in an old comedy, they are most wittily called <term>ἐσκοροδισμένοι</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed</gloss>, that is, one who has eaten garlic, used for someone vehement and too prone to fighting.

### *So that a bird does not fly high,*

Pull out the tail feathers that direct its course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *That a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way, they do not escape in aviaries.

<meta>continues from previous page: Each one</meta> is distinguished by piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if perceived by the eyes of true reason, and by the confidence of his own belief, standing out among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divinity as by its holiness and divine nature. Believe, O Asclepius, that this is the second god, governing all things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they are living or inanimate. For if the world is a living creature, always having been, being, and to be, there is nothing mortal in the world. For in every living part that is in the world, just as in one and the same animal that is always living, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live always. Therefore, just as the world is everlasting, so the sun is the eternal governor of vital things, or the frequent visitor and dispenser of all their vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living, or of the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed it once by an eternal law, granting life to all vital things in the manner which I shall describe.

<summary>This passage identifies the sun as the second god and the eternal governor of all living things within the world, emphasizing that the world itself is a living, immortal entity sustained by divine law.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, Sun, second god, world-soul, eternity, vitality, divine law, governance</keywords>

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> testifies that he saw these things. And there are things more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a cithara <note>a stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note>. At Megara, a certain rock, when struck, produces the sound of a stringed instrument; such is the great power of Music. It soothes the soul, elevates the mind, incites warriors to battle, and lightens the labors and fatigue of individual tasks. It recalls the fallen and the desperate, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by the singing of their guides. In a similar way, those carrying heavy burdens sing, and are made capable and relieved by it: for song produces delight and capability, mitigates the irascible, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, and tempers the madness of the phrenetic, dissipating vain thoughts: hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be cured or induced in this way. For the good is innate to truth, together with life and light, and no avenger <note>referring to the forces of darkness or vice</note> has approached beyond this. Indeed, all the avenging powers were cast out by a certain sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the manner of this very regeneration. The intellectual generation is composed by the presence of the number ten, which rejects the number twelve. And we have contemplated this from the generation itself. Whoever, therefore, because of the kindness of the generation which is according to God, loses his bodily sense, knows himself to be composed of divine things, and having become unswerving, rejoices in the divine power with his whole mind. **TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the intuition of the eyes, but by the act of the mind, which is exercised through inner strengths. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I would have you tell me this besides: how are the avenging shadows repelled by the ten powers from the number twelve? What is the method, Trismegistus? **TRISM.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve. And the numbers are eleven, and one which is omniform according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avenging powers are in a way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in a way joined, as for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to right reason, they are separated insofar as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. But life...

Therefore, the gods are the princes of all species; these are followed by the gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss>. These are sensible, of both origins, and similar to one another; they accomplish all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating its own work through the other. Of the heavens, or whatever is comprehended by that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. The <term>ousiarches</term> of the sun is light. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars <note>original: "xxxvi"</note> (whose name is <term>Horoscopij</term> <gloss>horoscopes/ascendants</gloss>) that are always fixed in the same place, their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphon</term> <gloss>all-formed</gloss> or Omniform. He makes diverse forms for diverse species. The seven spheres that are called erratic <note>meaning "wandering," referring to the planets</note> have <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>princes of essence</gloss>, that is, their own princes, which they call fortune, <term>eimarmenēs</term> <gloss>fate/destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, by the law of nature, with the firmest stability and varied by eternal agitation. The air, indeed, is the organ or machine of all things, through which all things are made. Moreover, the <term>ousiarches</term> of this is second, to mortals mortal things, and to these similar things. Therefore, with these things being so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected in such a way that mortal things are annexed to mortals, and sensible things to sensible things. But the sum of governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, or rather, they are one. For all things depend from the one, and flow down from it rather; when they are distant, they are believed to be many, divided. But when gathered, they are one, or rather two: from whence all things are made, and by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they are made, and from his will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: This is again the reason, O Trismegistus. TRISMEGISTUS: Such it is, O Asclepius. For God, either as father or lord...

Indeed, arsenic certainly cannot be fixed at all, unless the operating artist has an equal knowledge of its coloring spirit, in which matter all philosophers have slumbered, attempting in vain to effect anything from it. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the virtue by which it might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention has been made is derived from a false foundation, and by it, copper is falsely whitened, not transmuted. Sophists, having masked and painted Venus <note>alchemical term for copper</note> in this manner, mixed it with double its weight of Luna <note>alchemical term for silver</note>, and sold it to goldsmiths and moneyers; finally, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters, not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the sophists, in place of white, took red arsenic, and this itself went into a false art. For in whatever way it may be prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Some have proceeded further, to common sulfur, which they cooked so yellow with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines, day and night, until it emerged white. where they should have taken <term>pyrites</term> <gloss>a metallic mineral</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials, they took instead materials in which there is no operation. Although these things are expensive in the shops, they are of no value at all in the work. Our material, however, is not bought in any shop, yet it is found there daily, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the artisans labor. For our stone is indeed our <term>salt</term>, our <term>Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and infinite other things of this kind, yet not dug from wild, rural mountains with hammers and other tools. But our stone is extracted solely from our own mountains and springs. In our <term>Salt-spring</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, or rural mountains, which the artisans do not understand, nor can they believe or comprehend. For the Lord has obscured and closed their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to have been used, and they did not aim at the target at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in this contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. For when they should have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> with a strong fire; they scorched the <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong water/nitric acid</gloss>, and they immediately burned the operation of nature and the substances themselves, reducing them to nothing. When they should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> instead, and again, like those unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully and fell into doubt, and with lying words they kept saying that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they themselves are deservedly lying. For their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, which must be imputed to their own obscure and murky cunning, while, according to their own dark intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pseudo-philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning, and they reduced the things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. <meta>continues from previous page: ...the time</meta> requires the temperance of fire, and the succession of that increase little by little, with caution, until it is fixed in its lime, so that it does not easily return into a body, so that a greater fire may be administered to it, for the perfection of its lime. Likewise, let him not happen to err in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction, so that if at any time he places its lime into reduction, it happens to him that it does not reduce, but he finds it of its former disposition or reduced into glass, and he deems its reduction impossible. For we say that if he does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great one, it does not necessarily happen that it reduces, but it is possible to reduce it into vitrification <note>glass-like state</note>. And that is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive substance of <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss> included in the depth of its nature. If it draws out a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be more apt to be converted to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. And therefore it is necessarily left that, with the most rapid impetus of fire, he hastens to reduce it quickly. Otherwise, it is not reduced. Therefore, let him practice at that, and he will know.

The second mode of calcination of these two bodies, <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>tin</gloss>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity, very often in their fusion, and let it be mixed by much agitation with an iron rod, over the fire, until they are turned into ash through the mixture of salt. And afterwards, let their lime be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is converted to powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

<summary>This page details the technical challenges of reducing tin and lead, specifically warning against the risk of vitrification caused by the loss of internal mercury, and describes a method of calcination using salt.</summary>

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from those highest parts their lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed is present in their minds along with their religion, therefore some Mohammed is always placed in their sight. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, above which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not the Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan. Because he had also been a Christian, he was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Others have since succeeded this Mohammed. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like a torch, so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to any but the Mohammedans.

830. The Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> does not come into view today. It was told to me that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as a god, he was cast out from his seat, which he had held under the Papists, and was sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. So that the sedition might be quelled, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared like those corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face tending toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink down.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and from that, the worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and furthermore, toward the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images. For this reason, they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say one thing but mutter three, and therefore that they divide Omnipotence and make three out of one and the one; and that they are like fauns with three horns, one for each god, and at the same time three for one, and that they pray in this way, chant in this way, and sound forth from their pulpits in this way.

832. The Mohammedans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love justice and do good from religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there, no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of the God of the Father. This faith is among them, through which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved unless they were born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire where it is, and they also find it. It is in this, that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made only the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> the book of their religion, and therefore Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled into their thoughts, and they follow him with some worship, they therefore think little of our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first about the origin of idolatries. Before that religion, there was idolatrous worship.

<summary>This page describes the spiritual status and placement of Mohammedans, noting their hostility toward the Christian doctrine of the Trinity and their own path to salvation through acknowledging the Lord's dominion. ### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon. Chap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon, namely the figure of a serpent between an airy and a fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter held the mid-heaven with that head, which image they affirm contributes much to the success of petitions. They wished to denote by that image a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit or genius</gloss>, and they wished to represent him through the image of a serpent. For the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this as a divine animal above all others, and celebrate its divine nature, because in it, above other animals, there exists a sharper and more ample spirit or fire. This fact is shown both by its swift movement, without any feet or hands or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews its age and becomes young again with extraordinary vigor. They made an image of the tail in a similar way, when the moon was eclipsed in the tail, or was badly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it for the purpose of inducing anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil genius. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden, double-linked belt, which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first of that name, King of Spain (whether knowingly or unknowingly). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be surrounded by a serpent. Having subsequently discovered the magic power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the mansions of the Moon. Chap. XLVI.

They also used to make images in the individual mansions of the Moon. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made an image in an iron ring of a black man dressed in sackcloth and girded, throwing a small lance with his right hand; they sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax and uttered imprecations. In the second, against the anger of a prince and for his reconciliation, they sealed in white wax and mastic an image of a crowned king, and fumigated it with wood of aloes. In the third, they made an image in a silver ring, the measure of which was square, and the figure of which was a woman well-dressed sitting on a chair, with her right hand raised above her head; they sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and aromatic nail <note>likely clove</note>. They asserted that this grants prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for vengeance and separation, enmity and malevolence, they sealed in red wax an image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, for placing love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated it with wood of aloes and amber. Furthermore, this assumption of a void leads to a repulsive conclusion for them, which is that the world must be eternal; for if it were created in time, it would require a void. As for the premise stating that the will can only result in a created object, that is not self-evident. This is because the will that is in act is simultaneous with the act of the object of the will itself, since the will is among the relative terms <note>original: *al-muḍāf*, a reference to the Aristotelian category of relation</note>. It has been clarified that when one of two relative terms exists in act, the other exists in act, such as father and son; and when one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. If the will that is in act is created in time, then the object of the will is necessarily created in time; and if the will that is in act is eternal, then the object of the will that is in act is eternal. As for the will that precedes the object of the will, it is the will that is in potentiality—meaning that whose object has not yet emerged into act, since the act necessitating the creation of the object of the will was not conjoined with that will. Therefore, it is clear that when its object emerges, it is in a state of existence in which it was not before the emergence of its object into act, since it was the cause of the occurrence of the object of the will through the mediation of the act. Thus, if the <term>Mutakallimūn</term> <gloss>theologians of speculative discourse</gloss> posited that the will is created in time, it would necessarily follow that the object of the will is created in time, and this is inevitable. Similar is that which Architas says, that if a heart is taken recently extracted from an animal, and while it is still warm and living it is suspended over a patient with quartan fever, it removes it. Thus, if anyone swallows the heart of a Hoopoe, or a Swallow, or a Weasel, or a Mole, while it is still alive and palpitating, it contributes to his memory, reminiscence, intellect, and divination. Hence arose the general precept that whatever things are to be collected from animals, whether stones, or limbs, or excrements, such as hair, dung, or hooves, these must be taken from the animals while they are still alive, and even, if possible, while they remain alive afterwards. Whence they instruct that when you collect the tongue of a Frog, you should return it alive into the water; if you collect the tooth or eye of a Wolf, do not kill the Wolf, and so on for similar cases. Thus Democritus teaches that if anyone extracts the tongue of a living sea-frog, with no other part of the body adhering to it, and having released the frog into the sea, places the tongue upon the heart of a sleeping woman, she will answer truly whatever she is asked. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs tied to a sick person before sunrise, in such a way that they are dropped into water while blind, will drive away tertian fevers; and they report that the same eyes, when tied with the flesh of a Nightingale in a deerskin, provide wakefulness, having put sleep to flight. Similarly, the sting of a Stingray tied to the navel is said to make childbirth easy.

### On the Reign of the Sun.

Now you are approaching the end of your work, and you have almost completed your task; now everything appears like pure gold <note>original: *auri obryzi*, meaning gold of the highest standard or refined gold.</note>, and the virgin's milk <note>original: *lac virginis*, a common alchemical term for a white, milky solvent or mercurial water.</note>, with which you imbibe this matter, becomes very citrine. Render immortal thanks now to God, the giver of all good things, who has brought the work thus far, and pray to Him as a suppliant that He may guide your counsel henceforth, lest by chance, in striving to hasten the work now almost perfect, you destroy it entirely. Consider now that you have waited for almost seven months, and it will not be sound to annihilate everything in a single hour. Therefore, be very cautious, and all the more so the closer you are to perfection. If you proceed cautiously, these notable things will occur to you: First, you will observe a certain citrine sweat on the body, and finally citrine vapors, with the body subsiding, tinged with violet, and sometimes with a dark purple. But the unlearned, and even nature itself, from whom the truth did not proceed, have failed to obtain gifts from the Lord, nor do they have the notion of the immortal God. Not listening to both the gods and divine men, they have rejected all the gods, but they have chosen not only not to hate the prohibited demons, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform the only things through which God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a procession toward him through imitation and instruction from him. For instruction purges the intellect, while imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He preached well that God is the Father, and he said with what morals he should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the saints is praised or blamed. But it is only among Christians, or it is slandered as much as the demons—whom they opine to be gods—desire; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in the theaters and temples for the sake of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is a building up and where there is a ruin of morals. But who said this to him, or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians would rather revere than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love along with the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, whom we consider most blessed as citizens, forbids that sacrifices be made to others in the law which he gave to his people, the Hebrews; and he threatened very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated." And lest anyone think that it was commanded not to sacrifice to the worst demons and earthly spirits—whom he calls mimes or lesser ones—because they were also called gods in the holy scriptures, not by the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but by the Gentiles, which the seventy interpreters clearly set down in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons," lest anyone therefore think that it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but that it was permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, either to all or to some, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps someone, because he says "to the Lord alone," might believe that there is only one God to whom one thinks one must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in that way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony, gave a law to his people, the Hebrews, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but already spread among all the Gentiles, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, except to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of his and in his prophets to search for many things about this matter? Rather, there is no need to search. For they are not hidden or erased, but are open and frequent to collect, and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he wished for the true and supreme God to be sacrificed to by no one at all except to himself alone. Behold, this one thing, briefly—or rather, grandly and menacingly, but truthfully—said by that God whom their most learned men preach: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," he says, "shall be eradicated, except to the Lord only." Not that he needs anything, but because it is expedient for us that we be his. For it is sung to him in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, you are my God, for you do not need my goods." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of this one is we ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have disputed in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future were to cease, and that the Gentiles would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to its setting, just as we now see being done.

The matter in which the Lord God is recognized is that they are performed through all the attributes, which are completed by the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. As you will find in the creation of the first man, and in his judgment, and in his expulsion, and in all those matters, you will find that they all came about through the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy. Everything is in complete perfection, with Mercy and Justice, all as is appropriate in true judgment. According to this principle, the Torah says, "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The explanation of the verse is as follows: The Rock, who decrees judgment with strength, does not act with cruelty. He does not decree the judgment except that "His work is perfect," meaning the judgment He decreed was previously consulted with the two attributes, Loving-kindness <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness/Grace</gloss> and Justice. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect," for the word "perfect" <term>tamim</term> <gloss>perfect/whole</gloss> is the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins" <term>te'umim</term> <gloss>twins</gloss>, but in honorable language, it uses the word "perfect" for the two things above, and below it uses the word "twins." Thus it says, "And they shall be twins" <note>Exodus 26:24</note> below, "they shall be perfect" <note>Exodus 26:24</note> at the top. Below, they are twins; above, they are perfect. This is because below they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, like a helper and an accuser. But above, everything is one intention. Whether it is the helper or the accuser, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and no partiality, but only true judgment. Therefore, it says "His work is perfect," for He consulted with Justice and Mercy and decreed the judgment, and this is the secret of true judgment. Regarding what is said, "For all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, it means everything is for the eye of every beholder, as it says, "For all His ways are justice." You already know that justice is included in Justice and Mercy, for justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the middle line, the one who mediates between the two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Loving-kindness, Isaac to Justice, and Jacob decides between them, "a plain man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. Justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Loving-kindness on the side of Abraham and from Justice on the side of Isaac. Thus it says, "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have made" <note>Psalms 99:4</note>. The prophet said, "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The explanation of the verse is: "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice," what he said "but" <term>akh</term> <gloss>but/only</gloss> divides, meaning in half the attribute of justice, which is Loving-kindness, for justice is half Justice and half Loving-kindness. Therefore he said "but with justice," and said afterwards "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," and revealed the secret to diminish half of the justice from the side of anger. Therefore, justice depends on Jacob, who is the father of the tribes. He knew great sorrow for his children when the Holy One, blessed be He, decreed upon them, so he would seek mercy and righteousness for them. The secret is, "And the Lord of Hosts is exalted in justice" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written after it? "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. This means when the Lord of Hosts is exalted in justice, He rests the Justice and makes room for the attribute of God <term>El</term> <gloss>God (attribute of Mercy)</gloss>, which is the secret of what is said, "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." In short, when the Lord of Hosts is exalted in justice, the attribute of God comes, which is above, and performs righteousness, and the justice is served. This is the secret of what they said, that justice is included in Loving-kindness and Justice, and it says, "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have made." The great secret is, "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalms 89:15</note>, for righteousness is sometimes Justice, according to its reception of the flow, as explained, for righteousness is great Justice in strength. But when justice participates with it, then the throne is established in Mercy. And if He is exalted in justice, and reaches until Loving-kindness and Truth together, they are called the "shining faces," then everything is made into great Mercy, and this is the secret of "They shall precede..."

### **Torah** Light. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Service, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the commandment of "You shall not add and you shall not diminish," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which points to the perfection of the Torah. It is as the philosophers said: a thing that is perfect in the ultimate sense of perfection, it is not appropriate to say it is lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it were to receive an addition, it would be found that it was not perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that it has neither lack nor excess. It is known that the Torah depends on His Great Name, which is <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss>, "The Torah of the Lord is perfect," <note>Psalm 19:8</note> as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate <term>Shevuot</term> <gloss>Oaths</gloss>, in the chapter "Torah Light." And as it is written in the <term>Zohar</term> <gloss>Book of Splendor</gloss> on this verse, "This is My Name and this is My memorial." <note>Exodus 3:15</note> <term>Yod-He</term> with "My Name" equals 365. <term>Vav-He</term> with "My memorial" equals 248. And it is written, "I am the first and I am the last." <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> He is the absolute perfect; there is no deficiency in Him nor addition. Regarding this comes the warning, "You shall not do so to the Lord your God," <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> a warning against erasing the Name or smashing a stone from the Temple. The letters of the Name are in the house where He, may He be blessed, dwells; and likewise the Temple. It is written, "I am the Lord, My Name is..." The letters are like a closure for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul for them. He who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Service refers to most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place, and he came to the Chosen House and said a word with reason: "To His habitation you shall seek and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" hints at the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the Name <term>Yod-Vav</term>, as it is written, "And He descended upon Mount Sinai," <note>Exodus 19:20</note> and as it is written, "Do not fear, for it will dwell with me," for in the Temple the Glory is unified in the splendor of His people. This is "To His Name, His Name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> says, "To cause His Shekhinah to dwell." And around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>husk/shell of impurity</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings in any place that you see." <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>

### **And sometimes** sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inward. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn and the sacrifice from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written regarding them, "There you shall offer," <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note> meaning there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. Since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where holiness is, we were commanded to be "turn from evil" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> and to destroy all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate after them, and this is commanded specifically in the Holy Land. Its secret is a hint to the ten nations, for their power is not that of idolaters. The matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the rule of the Honored Name, worship the Name by "cutting the shoots," <note>a metaphor for heresy</note> and this is actual idolatry. However, those in the lands outside the Land of Israel are under the rule of the external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against smashing one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and lose a "subverted city" <note>Deuteronomy 13:13</note> and not to build it again, for its place is impure. Likewise, an inciter and a seducer must be uprooted and eradicated, for he is from the impurity of the primordial serpent who was an inciter. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent," therefore the powers of the inciter are not revived. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, like the matter said regarding the serpent, "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." <note>Genesis 3:15</note> Also, a false prophet is like an inciter. Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the firstborn, that the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the firstborn, which are the "first," point to great holiness, as I have written elsewhere. Therefore, they shall go to the holy place, and from there they shall take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of the "lesser holy things" and the "second tithe" is that their eating is in Jerusalem. This is the "grain, wine, and oil," which are the fathers of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat the lesser holy things until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul. Afterward, there is permission to eat and to enjoy. Know that just as the service, which is the sacrifice, is a sacrifice to the Lord, so is the servant, for the essence of the service is that he sacrifices himself, in the secret of "When a man among you brings an offering." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> And the burnt offering is entirely consumed, for it comes upon the thought of "turning from evil," the thought which is spiritual, and he is... all the night, etc., the serpent does not hinder him. And the lesser holy things are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **And the secret** of the firstborn is the secret of the holy people of Israel, who are called, as it is written, "Israel is My firstborn." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> He has compassion on them, "And you shall guard them," and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating the holy things is against the blemishes and the defects in them, for the holy people of Israel are called "man," and he is a holy creation. Afterward, a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and he was clothed in "garments of skin," but he has a redemption, in the secret of "And I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:3</note> This was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <note>the scapegoat</note>, "And he shall bear their iniquities." The meaning is that they fall upon his head and upon his people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy things in order to eat them, for he who causes a blemish in the holy things by his own choice... also the prohibition of work and shearing in the holy things, for even the broken tablets are holy.

### **The sum** of the matter is that the service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the man. Likewise, his soul is called after his death to the altar above, and Michael is the High Priest. The matter is the secret that "in the image of God was man made." Therefore, the warning came to be careful in his life regarding the taking of lives, not to kill a man except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then it is "by the hands of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness and He is the judge," for the Lord, may He be blessed, is a true witness and a true judge. So the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <gloss>High Court</gloss> must be: just as they are true judges, so they must be true witnesses. I mean to say that they must have the secret of the truth of the witnesses in complete clarity, that is, the inquiry and investigation. Then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven, and "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones." <note>Psalm 116:15</note>

### **And since** "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones," for the holy people of Israel are holy from the side of their souls, which after their death the souls cleave above, therefore the command came, "You shall not cut yourselves, you shall not make any baldness," etc., <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note> for "You are children to the Lord your God." This is not so for the nations; the cutting and the baldness are from their customs, for it is appropriate since in their death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world or in the world to come. This is not so for us, the children of the living God. When one departs from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, on the contrary, we have a permanent dwelling above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to increase mourning and to perform these acts.

### **Let us return** to the matter that the man who serves is himself the sacrifice, as it is written, "When a man among you brings an offering." There is another secret in this, for the "man" who is slaughtered, even below, the man, that is, in the secret of the transmigration, "Man and beast You shall save, O Lord." <note>Psalm 36:7</note> Therefore, even in the eating of ordinary meat, the meat of desire, we were commanded in the slaughtering and in great care without a notch, for then it is a carcass, and then it becomes a carcass in Israel. For who knows what transmigration is in it? "Love your neighbor as yourself" <note>Leviticus 19:18</note>—choose for him a beautiful death, that is, slaughtering without a notch. If the animal dies by itself, or it spreads and the power of impurity takes hold of it... but when he slaughters it properly, and there is in the animal, its sacrifice, and like a pure bird, a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **And he who eats** a limb from a living creature is like one who eats from the flesh of "that which is," when there is a transmigration of a soul there. **Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: A heifer in its first year, and a cow in its second year. And the Sages say: A heifer in its second year, and a cow in its third or fourth year. Rabbi Joshua said: I have not heard regarding the "third." They said to him: What is the language of "third"? He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain. They said to him: What is the language of "fourth-year"? He said to them: Thus I heard it without explanation. Ben Azzai said: I will explain. If you say "fourth" to another in counting, and when you say "fourth-year," it is four years old. Regarding the likeness of the offspring, one may doubt what the cause is why sometimes the fetus is found to be more like the father, sometimes the mother, and sometimes even like the progenitors, whether paternal or maternal; especially when, in one act and at the same moment, several eggs are fertilized. It is also admirable that virtues and vices, and even diseases, stigmata, and birthmarks, are transferred from the parents to the descendants; and this in only some fetuses, not in all. In the chicken genus, some are noble and born for battle; they prefer to die rather than yield to adversaries by fleeing: yet their descendants, unless they are begotten by similar parents, gradually lose that virtue; according to the saying: the brave are created from the brave. In most other species of animals (and especially in humans) the nobility of the kind is observed; and many gifts of mind and body arrive by transmission.

I have often wondered why, when we see the offspring (for the most part) obtain a certain mixed structure or composition from both parents, and this in all other parts; yet the same does not happen in the genitals: but usually either a male or a female is born, and very rarely a hermaphrodite?

Finally, many things exist before they appear; and some are begun among the first, which are completed last; such as the eyes, the genitals, and the beak.

They argue further: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain occult virtues following the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also acquire some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects, and thus it is not illicit to use them and other things of this kind. Furthermore, demons can transform bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in the third book of <term>De Trinitate</term> <gloss>On the Trinity</gloss>, and this is evident in the bewitched. <meta>continues from previous page</meta> with other things. The one being purged must not hasten to consume many or poor-quality foods, lest nature attract them undigested. If something of that sort is necessary, it must be in very small amounts, spaced out so that it is gradual, and what enters the body must be well-digested. Phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for evacuation specific to a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is something other than phlebotomy. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. If the cessation of diarrhea causes a habitual ailment, it is often because that evacuation is being repeated, such as when the cessation of a nosebleed causes blockages; repeating it removes them. Know that the remainder of the material that needs to be purged is less susceptible to being tracked down and reached until the strength fails. Nature often dissolves that remainder itself. As long as the humor is of the type that is appropriate and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess. You may sometimes need to purge until fainting occurs. For one whose strength is great and whose bad humors are abundant, purge him little by little. The same applies if the material is highly matured or strongly mixed with blood and cannot be purged all at once. This is the case in sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that diarrhea draws from above and clears from below, so it is consistent with the familiar attraction. It is also consistent after the materials have settled; if the materials are from below, it draws them to it in opposition and clears them from where they are, and this is by the action of attraction and vice versa. The state of phlebotomy varies according to the places from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good digestion, and the inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

We say: It is recommended for one who wishes to be purged to consume or space out his food, and to determine the amount he will experience in a day in portions, and to make them different foods and different drinks. The stomach is affected by this state, such that it desires to push what is in it upward or downward. As for food that is not varied, but rather one food after another, the stomach becomes satisfied with it, relaxes, and grips it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for one with a naturally loose constitution, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur to one who has a good regimen; he needs what is lighter than that. Exercise, massage, and cupping may suffice for him. Then, if his body is filled with the greatest fullness of the best humors, meaning blood, then phlebotomy is what is needed for purification, not diarrhea. If necessity dictates phlebotomy or evacuation, such as in autumn, and the patient is one who vomits, then he should be purged by vomiting rather than phlebotomy. This is one of the recommendations of Hippocrates and the books that follow it, and it is the truth. Likewise, if the phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. But if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, phlebotomy might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In short, if the humors are equal, prioritize phlebotomy; if a need for evacuation arises after that, then purge. If they are not equal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform phlebotomy. Whoever prioritizes medicine over phlebotomy should have prioritized phlebotomy, even if only a little. Whoever was recently phlebotomized and needed evacuation, and drank medicine, it was stopped for him. Often, drinking the medicine when phlebotomy was required resulted in fainting and agitation. If it does not subside with sedatives, then phlebotomy should have been prioritized. There is no evacuation needed for excessive fullness that is not called for by the severity of the ailment and the fullness according to quality and quantity. Often, a good regimen replaces the phlebotomy required at the time. Often, the need for evacuation arises, but an obstacle opposes it; the only solution is fasting, sleep, and correcting the dyscrasia <note>imbalance of humors</note> by way of fullness. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other things at a known time, especially in the spring. It is necessary to take precautions before its time and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be phlebotomy or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines is a form of evacuation, such as what is done for those with dropsy. You may be forced to use a medicine that is homogeneous to the humor being purged in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>a purgative resin</gloss> when you need to purge yellow bile. In that case, you must mix with it something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>a dried fruit used as a laxative</gloss>. Correcting the dyscrasia if it occurs afterward in those with visceral tumors weakens their diarrhea. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the purgative and <term>cassia fistula</term> <gloss>a mild laxative</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that easily responds to vomiting, the first step in his purification is to use vomiting in summer or spring when it is time, for that relieves the body of fatigue." Know that the one who is accustomed to a loose constitution or is not accustomed to vomiting should avoid it in times when it is not needed. It is necessary to prepare before diarrhea by softening the humor one wishes to purge and widening the passages at that time, for that relieves the body of fatigue. Know that the one who is accustomed to a loose constitution or is not accustomed to vomiting, before using strong medicine, should use one of the regimens that reduce and purge. Diarrhea with abdominal emaciation is difficult and tiring. The purgative medicine may return as a laxative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk during intense hunger, or if the drinker has a loose constitution, or because of the medicine, or if the medicine is heavier in substance than what descends quickly. The purgative may remain stagnant due to the weakness of the stomach, or the intensity of the weight, or because the medicine causes distress, or because the person has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge the undigested matter, stirs up the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it in the body, so it takes hold of the body and attracts other humors to it, and that humor increases in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as yellow bile. Some are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a state like milk and stars; its diarrhea is more correct in itself. Whoever has a humor that is descending, such as those with intestinal slippage, the contraction of the intestines hinders the purgative medicine. What is composed of medicines that are highly different in the time of diarrhea causes the diarrhea to be agitated, and the first purges the second before the second purges, and perhaps the first purges the second itself. Whoever is exposed to diarrhea and his body is not purified by it, he must have colic and distress, and what is purged is purged with great difficulty. In short, the medicine that purges the superfluities does not cause agitation. If it is taken with agitation, it either purges what is not a superfluity, or if the purged humor changes from vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended to be purged.

May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that we keep Your statutes in this world and merit to live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the days of the Messiah and for the life of the world to come. So that my glory may sing to You and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord forever and ever, for in the Lord God is the Rock of ages. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. He desires, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious.

O Lord our Master, how glorious is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

And now, may the power of the Lord be great, as You have spoken, saying: Remember Your mercies and Your kindnesses, for they are from of old.

May His great name be magnified and sanctified in the world that He created according to His will. May He establish His kingdom, cause His salvation to sprout, and bring near <note>another reading: the end of</note> His Messiah, in your lifetime and in your days and in the lifetime of the entire house of Israel, speedily and in a near time, and say: Amen. May His great name be blessed forever and to all eternity. Blessed, praised, glorified, exalted, extolled, honored, elevated, and lauded be the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, above <note>from the time and above all</note> all blessings and songs, praises and consolations that are uttered in the world, and say: Amen. Accept, accept with mercy and favor our prayer. May the prayer and supplication of the entire house of Israel be accepted before their Father who is in heaven, and say: Amen. May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever.

May there be great peace from heaven, and life, upon us and upon all Israel, and say: Amen. My help is from the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth. He who makes peace in His high places, He shall make peace upon us and upon all Israel, and say: Amen.

A prayer of David. Incline Your ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am pious; save Your servant, You, my God, who trusts in You. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long. Gladden the soul of Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in kindness to all who call upon You. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplications. In the day of my trouble I will call upon You, for You will answer me. There is none like You among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like Yours. All the nations that You have made shall come and bow down before You, O Lord, and they shall glorify Your name. For You are great and do wonders; You alone are God. Teach me, O Lord, Your way; I will walk in Your truth; unite my heart to fear Your name. I will thank You, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify Your name forever. For Your kindness is great toward me, and You have delivered my soul from the lowest depths of the grave. O God, the insolent have risen against me, and a congregation of violent men have sought my soul, and they have not set You before them. But You, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness and truth. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give Your strength to Your servant and save the son of Your handmaid. Show me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be ashamed, because You, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

O house of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the peoples will walk, each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and ever.
May the Lord our God be with us as He was with our fathers; may He not forsake us and not abandon us. To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments and His statutes and His ordinances which He commanded our fathers. And may these my words, which I have supplicated before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, to do the judgment of His servant and the judgment of His people Israel, as each day requires. So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord is God; there is no other.

A song of ascents of David. If it had not been the Lord who was for us, let Israel now say: If it had not been the Lord who was for us when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive in the heat of their anger against us. Then the waters would have overwhelmed us; the torrent would have gone over our soul. Then the raging waters would have gone over our soul. Blessed be the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. Our soul has escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare was broken, and we have escaped. Our help is in the name of the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth.

What, therefore, is the manner in which God foreknows these uncertain future events? For if He deems that things are avoidable in the future, when it is not possible for them to happen, He is deceived; and to think this is not only a sin, but even to suggest it is wrong. But if He discerns that they will be in such a way that He knows they can either happen or not happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias, who said, "Whatever I say will either be or not be"? Why, then, would divine prudence differ from human opinion if, like men, it judges uncertain things whose outcome is uncertain? But if, in that most certain fountain of all things, there is nothing uncertain...

# Question

The third article. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It is proceeded thus. That more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us, and simple things are posterior. But universals are prior; therefore, they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and the parts are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later to us. Furthermore, effects are known before causes and principles. But universals are known later to us. But if it is that, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*, we must proceed from the general to the singular. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, and intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known in act and in a certain way in potency. As the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, both the whole in which parts are contained in potency and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the animal in which there is rational or irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "man." And it falls to reason if I compare whatever is more or less, just as sense goes from potency to act, so does the intellect; this is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition that appears in the sense. For more is known in the sense, and it is divided more, and when less is known, it is more remote through <unclear>the being of the body</unclear>, and <unclear>the being of the body</unclear> and "animal"; and more is known as "being animal" and <unclear>the being of the body</unclear> and <unclear>the good</unclear> and prior <unclear>good</unclear> and <unclear>sort</unclear>. Or it pleases and is evident that a child from the beginning first distinguishes <unclear>good</unclear> and <unclear>from the good</unclear>; and in children from the beginning they call all men "fathers." Later, however, he terminates each one, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: for he knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or he knows <unclear>the fiction</unclear> and the principle, and thus he knows <unclear>the genus</unclear> and is able to know <unclear>the species</unclear>. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior to us, and the cognition of the universal is sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If both sense and intellect are considered, the cognition of the less and the common is prior. To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in a twofold way. One way is that it is considered according to the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true is the same, it has a relation to many things. It arrives at the abstraction of the intellect, and this is the end, while the true is posterior. In the first book of *De Anima*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior: but <unclear>he placed</unclear> universals as substances; and in this consideration, it is true: more because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting things, which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of man and animal. For the animal is generated before the man, as the Philosopher says in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. Another is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature to that which is in potency, and by this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for the intention of nature does not rest in the generation of the animal, but intends to generate the man. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole, it becomes more universal, not only <unclear>the common</unclear> but also man and horse; as it can be, the less universal is contained in the future, not only the more universal but also others, as man is not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so through its reason. To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is <unclear>the house</unclear>. In another way, when it is a part of this whole, and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition to be considered absolutely is prior to us and is defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things. But rather, they are the parts.

When the Lion awoke the next morning, the judge entered with a group of prominent companions, carrying the document containing the excuses Dimna had provided. The Lion took the document and ordered them to leave him.

He then sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion replied, "I will not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you distinguish between what harms you and what benefits you. I fear that by continuing to deliberate on Dimna’s case, you will stir up a situation you will be unable to manage or withstand."

She then stood up and left in anger. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life once the accusation has settled in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt. This will free your neck from the consequences in the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you for two reasons: first, your ability to find exits and fabricate excuses that defend yourself; and second, your voluntary confession of guilt, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: 'Death in a state of honor is better than life in a state of disgrace.'"

Dimna answered him, saying, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. You know that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I have knowledge of myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your eyes—if that is indeed the case—because you suspect that I have striven..."

If you leave two sisters and a wife, and he bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the money after the bequest, the method for this is to establish the estate at twelve shares. For each sister, there is a third of what remains of the money after the bequest. This is money minus a bequest. You know that one-eighth of what remains with the bequest equals a sister's portion. So, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the money minus one-eighth of a bequest. One-eighth of the money minus one-eighth of a bequest, together with the bequest, equals a sister's portion. That is one-eighth of the money and seven-eighths of a bequest. The entire money equals three-eighths of the money and three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths of the money from the money, and there remain five-eighths of the money, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The entire money equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The money is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of bequest, a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another, a quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from a third.

Therefore, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If a judge exerts himself and gets it right, he has two rewards, and if he gets it wrong, he has one reward." And what judge is greater than one who judges concerning existence that it is such-and-such or not such-and-such? These judges are the scholars whom God has singled out for interpretation. This error that is overlooked in the Law is only the error that occurs to scholars when they examine difficult matters which the Law has tasked them with investigating. As for the error that occurs from someone other than this class of people, it is pure sin. Whether the error is in theoretical or practical matters, if a judge who is ignorant of the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>prophetic tradition</gloss> errs in a ruling, he is not excused. Likewise, the one who judges existing things, if the conditions for judgment are not found in him, he is not excused; rather, he is either a sinner or an infidel. If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the causes of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him, namely knowledge of the fundamentals and knowledge of how to derive rulings from those fundamentals by <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>, how much more so should this be required for the one who judges existing things, namely to know the rational first principles and the way of deriving from them? In short, error in the Law is of two kinds: either an error for which the person who is qualified to investigate that matter is excused, just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, and a skilled judge is excused if he errs in a ruling, but the one who is not of that standing is not excused; or an error for which no one among people is excused, but rather, if it occurs in the foundations of the Law, it is <term>kufr</term> <gloss>infidelity</gloss>, and if it occurs in what is beyond the foundations, it is <term>bid'ah</term> <gloss>innovation</gloss>. 3223. There are two lights from which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to be of that light, still are; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus they have some form only by the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man are so essential that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. The light of heaven, however, is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has only a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, and not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This light, namely the light of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Those things that in the light of the world make one ray, in the light of heaven make myriads. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no apperception at all, for the things that belong to the light of the world have life from that source. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual man—that is, when the former serves the latter. The things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and a fraction, so the Jewish method of working with temporal hours <note>unequal hours that vary by season</note> does not hold unless the conjunction for the beginning of Tishrei occurs at the autumnal equinox. It never occurs with it, but rather precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have explained previously. Once we have extracted the time of the conjunction using the calculation that the Jews provided in the table we analyzed according to their view, we ascend from that to the knowledge of the beginning of the year and the understanding of its nature regarding deficiency, moderation, and fullness. We have already gained knowledge of whether it is a common or a leap year. We then search in the table of limits for a duration of days of the week whose boundaries encompass the time at which the conjunction occurred for us, in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for common years if it is a common year. Once we find it, we discover alongside it the beginning of the year from the week and its nature. When we know the beginning of the year and its nature, and we combine that nature with the common or leap year, we know from that the passage of the beginning of the next year.
